null-vs-empty.notApplicableReason: The only text column, Product.Name, is NOT NULL, so no NULL text value can be sent. '' is attacked in the names case; a NULL check date and a NULL start product are attacked separately.

collation-case.notApplicableReason: The only text input is Production.Product.Name, which the source keeps unique under its case-insensitive collation (AK_Product_Name), so two products whose names differ only in case cannot exist. The procedure compares no text: it joins and filters on integer keys and dates.

cases.reasoning: @CheckDate is datetime: '2020-06-30T00:00:00.001' becomes .000 (1/300 s ticks) and @CheckDate <= ISNULL(EndDate, @CheckDate) holds. The PostgreSQL parameter is timestamp and keeps .001, which is after EndDate, so the anchor row for product 2 may be dropped.

cases.label: 27-edge chain whose last edge ends at 23:59:59.999: SQL Server rounds it into use, reaches recursion level 26 and stops with error 530
cases.reasoning: Whether MAXRECURSION 25 is exceeded depends on the date filter of the 27th edge. SQL Server stores its EndDate 23:59:59.999 as the next midnight, so the edge is in use at the check date and the walk needs 26 recursions (error 530). A PostgreSQL column or parameter that kept .999 would drop that edge, need only 25 recursions, and return 26 rows (one per remaining edge) instead of raising.

cases.reasoning: @CheckDate >= StartDate is UNKNOWN for NULL, and ISNULL(EndDate, NULL) keeps it UNKNOWN. A conversion that defaulted a NULL check date (e.g. to now()) or used COALESCE(check_date, ...) would return rows.

cases.reasoning: b.ProductAssemblyID = NULL (or b.ComponentID = NULL) is never true. A row with a NULL ProductAssemblyID (a top-level product) is present; a conversion using IS NOT DISTINCT FROM would match it.

cases.label: a diamond (1 -> 2 -> 4, 1 -> 3 -> 4) and 4 -> 5: the 4 -> 5 rows reached by two paths at one recursion level are summed
cases.reasoning: Both paths reach the 4 -> 5 edge at recursion level 2 with the same BOMLevel, cost and price, so GROUP BY merges them and SUM(PerAssemblyQty) adds 1.45 twice (2.90). Quantities are at or above the source minimum 1.00 and end in 5 (1.05, 1.15, 1.25, 1.35, 1.45); costs end in .0005 and are not negative. Any rounding of the decimal(8,2) sum or of the money columns would show.

cases.reasoning: RecursionLevel is in the GROUP BY, so 3 -> 4 gives two rows that share BOMLevel, ProductAssemblyID and ComponentID and differ only in RecursionLevel (1 and 2). Their relative order is not defined; the rows themselves must match.

cases.label: BOMLevel out of step with depth: 32767 (smallint maximum), 1 and 16384 on a three-edge chain
cases.reasoning: ORDER BY BOMLevel uses the stored value, not the depth, so the depth-2 row (BOMLevel 1) sorts first and the depth-1 row (32767) last; a conversion that ordered by recursion level would differ. 32767 checks the smallint mapping; the source requires BOMLevel >= 1 for a row with an assembly, so no lower extreme is sent. Product names are distinct (unique in the source); the products share StandardCost and ListPrice, a non-key tie.

cases.label: product names with a trailing space, an empty name, non-ASCII text and a 50-character name are returned as stored
cases.reasoning: ComponentDesc is the component (b.ComponentID)'s Name and is in the GROUP BY. 'Nut ' ends in a space that SQL Server returns (it ignores it only in comparisons); a char(n) mapping or an rtrim would drop it. '' (empty, not NULL), an accent, an emoji and a 50-character name check the nvarchar(50) -> varchar(50) mapping. Names differing only in case are not sent: Production.Product.Name is unique under the case-insensitive source collation, so two such products cannot exist (see notApplicable).

cases.label: a quantity summed past decimal(8,2): three in-use 999999.99 rows for one pair give 2999999.97; large money costs ending in 5
cases.reasoning: SUM(decimal(8,2)) is decimal(38,2) in T-SQL, so three 999999.99 rows (same pair, StartDates 00:00, 06:00 and 12:00 on 2020-01-01, all in use at the check date) sum to 2999999.97; a conversion that kept numeric(8,2) for the sum would overflow. StandardCost 900719925474.0985 and ListPrice 900719925474.0990 are large non-negative money values (the source requires >= 0) that the harness can capture exactly; they check money -> numeric(19,4) without rounding the last digit. The second component has quantity 1.05 and cost 0.0005.

cases.label: product ids with gaps and at the int limits: 1 -> 1000 -> 2147483647, with -2147483648 and 0 unused
cases.reasoning: ProductID is the key of Product; the walk follows 1, 1000 and 2147483647, with unrelated products 0 and -2147483648 present. recursion_level + 1 and the integer columns must not overflow or be narrowed.

cases.label: a cycle reached only through an edge that is not in use at the check date, and an unreachable cycle: rows, no recursion error
cases.reasoning: 2 -> 3 -> 2 would be a cycle, but 3 -> 2 was in use only from 2019-01-01 to 2019-12-31; 5 <-> 6 is a cycle the walk never reaches. SQL Server applies the date filter in the recursive member, so it never recurses past level 1. The PostgreSQL walk must apply the same filter before counting levels, or it raises 54001.

cases.label: a product missing in the middle of the walk: its row is dropped and the walk does not continue below it
cases.reasoning: The recursive member joins Product on the component (b.ComponentID); product 3 has no Product row, so 2 -> 3 is not produced and 3 -> 4 is never reached. A conversion that recursed on BillOfMaterials alone and joined Product afterwards would list 3 -> 4.

cases.label: 26-edge chain whose last edge is in use only because datetime rounds its end 23:59:59.999 to midnight: exactly 25 recursions, allowed, 26 rows
cases.reasoning: MAXRECURSION 25 allows 25 recursions; this walk needs exactly 25 when the 26th edge is in use. Its EndDate 2020-01-01 23:59:59.999 is stored by datetime as 2020-01-02 00:00:00.000, equal to the check date, so SQL Server keeps it and returns 26 rows without error. A conversion that counted the limit one level too low would raise; one that kept .999 would drop the edge and return 25 rows.

objections.resolution: A05 now states that dropping the final edge leaves 26 rows. Its edge count and MAXRECURSION outcome match the sent chain.
